title: Understanding Grease Buildup in Kitchen Drains
description: An educational breakdown of how liquid fats and grease solidify inside drain lines, creating stubborn downstream blockages.
image_prompt: A detailed 3D technical cutaway illustration of a standard 1.5-inch white PVC drain pipe underneath a kitchen sink, vertical 9:16 aspect ratio. The cross-section shows the interior of the pipe where a thick, yellow-white layer of congealed grease and oil adheres to the lower and side inner walls, restricting the pipe inner diameter. Clear wastewater flows through the remaining narrowed center channel. Photorealistic plastic textures, realistic wall thickness, clean uncluttered light gray background beneath a sink cabinet, soft studio lighting focused on the interior pipe cross-section. Clean composition with empty space at the top and bottom third for text overlays. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermarks, no arrows, no diagrams on the image.
visual_story: The visual uses a clear cutaway view of a horizontal kitchen drain pipe to highlight what happens inside an unseen drainage line. Viewers can see how hot liquid fats cool down, adhere to cold pipe walls, and build up in layers, reducing the effective diameter of the pipe and catching debris.

on_image_text.hook: Why Hot Water Doesn't Stop Grease Clogs
on_image_text.explanation: Liquid fats travel down the drain, cool against cold pipe walls, and solidify downstream where water temperature drops.
on_image_text.callout: Congealed fat layer narrowing the 1.5-inch PVC pipe interior
on_image_text.takeaway: Wipe greasy pans into the trash before washing—never pour liquid fats down the sink.
